units.title: Ordered stages, stage cost and balanced or automated partitioning
outcomes: Partition an ordered layer stack over \(p\) stages with embedding-first and output-last ownership and a stated remainder rule.
Estimate per-stage cost from forward plus backward time and name the critical stage that sets the makespan.
Explain why hand-placed splits are not automatic graph partitioning and what an automatic partitioner would still decide.
units.why: A pipeline is only as fast as its slowest stage, and every later schedule assumes the partition. Placing embedding, layers and output head once, with cost attached, fixes the map the rest of the section executes.

next.note: Split batches into microbatches that flow across the stages built here.
Give each stage its parameters, loss and optimizer state from this partition map.

study.title: Manual and tracer model splits
study.locator: Step 1 (page read 2026-10-14): manual split deleting layers 4 to 7 or 0 to 3 with `ModuleDict` names kept, and tracer split with `SplitPoint.BEGINNING` at `layers.4` plus `build_stage`
study.depth: Stop after Step 1. Schedules and loss placement belong to later units.

focus: Stages are ordered and contiguous: microbatch \(i\) leaves stage \(s\) for stage \(s+1\) in both directions, so any partition is a cut plan over the layer list.
First and last stages carry extra cost: the embedding lookup lives on stage 0 and the final norm plus output projection live on the last stage, and a balance that ignores them overloads both ends.
Equal layer counts do not imply equal stage cost: position-dependent work such as the vocabulary projection, plus backward costing about twice forward, moves the critical stage.
The tracer `split_spec` still takes hand-placed split points; it automates cutting, not choosing where to cut.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, partition a 10-layer stack over 3 stages with the remainder-to-early-ranks rule, mark embedding and output ownership, and write each stage's layer list with its per-stage layer count.
traps: Counting the embedding, norm and output projection as free when balancing. Measure them as layers would be measured, or the end stages become the bottleneck.
Assuming equal layer counts balance the pipe. Estimate forward plus backward seconds per stage and balance those, not layer counts.
Calling a tracer `split_spec` an automatic partitioner. It places cuts you chose; a true partitioner would also choose cut positions from a cost model, and that stays later work.

selfTest.q: Split 10 layers over 3 stages with Picotron's remainder rule. Which layers land on each stage?
selfTest.a: Counts \([4, 3, 3]\): stage 0 holds layers 0 to 3, stage 1 holds 4 to 6, stage 2 holds 7 to 9. The \(10 \bmod 3 = 1\) remainder layer goes to the earliest rank.

selfTest.q: Why does the Playbook say pipeline parallelism saves no activation memory per GPU?
selfTest.a: Each stage holds \(1/p\) of the layers but \(p\) microbatches are in flight before the first backward, so the layer fraction times the microbatch count leaves activation memory about flat.

selfTest.q: Why does the tutorial split delete `ModuleDict` entries instead of rebuilding a smaller list?
selfTest.a: Deleting keeps fully qualified names stable, so checkpoints save and load and FQN-addressed services keep resolving. Reindexing shifts every name.

selfTest.q: A 12-layer model with `input_weight` 1 and `output_weight` 1 is split over 4 stages. How many transformer layers does each stage hold?
selfTest.a: 14 effective layers split \([4, 4, 3, 3]\), minus the end weights: \([3, 4, 3, 2]\), which sums to 12.

Draw the forward activation and backward gradient edges across stages and place the synchronous update.
State divisibility constraints and a remainder policy that keeps the loss mean correct.
units.why: Microbatches turn a sequential layer stack into a parallel schedule, but only if batch accounting and cross-stage dependencies are exact. Every bubble number and equivalence check later divides by these counts.

next.note: Run GPipe and 1F1B over this dependency graph.
Encode the graph as simulator events with validation checks.

study.locator: `pp_engine` branch calling the AFAB or 1F1B step with `grad_acc_steps` microbatches, and `MicroBatchDataLoader` with `global_batch_size` equal to microbatch size times `grad_acc_steps` times `dp_world_size`

study.title: Pipelining pseudocode and dependency walk
study.locator: Pipelining section: layer-by-layer forward with device handoffs, loss derivative seeding the backward walk, per-stage input-gradient and weight-gradient computation

focus: Global batch is a product: microbatch size times microbatch count times data-parallel degree, and token counts multiply by sequence length on top.
Forward edges carry activations to the next stage; backward edges carry input gradients to the previous stage; weights never move between stages.
The synchronous update sits after the last microbatch's gradients accumulate at mini-batch end, which is what makes the pipeline update match a large-batch update.
Equal microbatches keep every mean exact; a short tail microbatch needs explicit reweighting or padding, never silent averaging.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the global-batch equation and the forward and backward dependency edges for \(p\) stages and \(m\) microbatches: which forward output feeds which stage, which gradient flows back, and where the synchronous update sits.
traps: Reading the microbatch size as the global batch. Multiply by the microbatch count and the data-parallel degree first.
Letting a short last microbatch keep weight 1 in the loss mean. Size-weight it or pad it, or the update drifts from the oracle.
Starting backward before microbatch 0 reaches the last stage. The loss seed does not exist until then, so early backward calls have nothing to differentiate.

selfTest.q: Microbatch size 2, microbatch count 4, data-parallel degree 4. What is the global batch?
selfTest.a: \(2 \times 4 \times 4 = 32\) examples before any sequence-length factor.

selfTest.q: Where does the synchronous update sit in GPipe, and why does that placement matter?
selfTest.a: After gradients accumulate over all \(M\) microbatches at mini-batch end. That placement is what equates one pipelined step with one large-batch synchronous step.

selfTest.q: What happens on setting `MICRO_BATCH_SIZE` 3 with `LOCAL_BATCH_SIZE` 8 in the TorchFeather example?
selfTest.a: The divisibility guard raises. Either pad or re-split into equal microbatches, or implement a remainder policy that reweights the loss mean.

selfTest.q: In the JAX pipelining pseudocode, what is copied between devices on the forward pass and on the backward pass?
selfTest.a: Forward copies activations to the next device; backward copies the loss derivative with respect to the input to the previous device. Weights stay sharded per device.

Model each transfer as a simulator event with a matching rule.

study.title: Forward and backward handoffs between devices
study.locator: 06:06:14 to 06:11:12: layer groups per GPU, forward activation handoffs to the next device, and backward upstream-gradient handoffs to the previous device

focus: Each transfer is identified by direction plus microbatch: TorchFeather adds the microbatch index to a per-direction tag base so in-flight microbatches cannot match the wrong receive.
Picotron leans the other way: single ops on the default tag pair up in strict program order, so any rank-specific branch in the op sequence deadlocks the pair.
Shapes and dtypes are agreed out of band: the receiver allocates the buffer from `tensor_shapes` before the transfer, and a mismatch stalls rather than raising.
First and last stages skip one direction each: the first stage never receives forward, the last stage never receives backward, and the skip must be in the protocol, not just the compute.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a two-process gloo script where rank 0 sends an activation tensor forward with tag 100 plus microbatch index and rank 1 returns its gradient with tag 200 plus microbatch index, asserting shape and dtype on receipt.
traps: Reusing one tag for every microbatch and trusting call order. Tag per microbatch as TorchFeather does, or prove every rank runs an identical op sequence as Picotron requires.
Calling `torch.cuda.synchronize` after a gloo transfer on a CPU-only run. It raises when no GPU is present, so gate device sync on the backend instead of copying GPU code.
Posting a blocking send before the peer posts its receive on both ranks at once. Pair each send with a receive through one bidirectional call, or keep the recv-first order on both sides.

selfTest.q: Why do TorchFeather tags add the microbatch index to the base instead of using one tag per direction?
selfTest.a: Several microbatches are in flight at once, so one tag per direction could match a receive with the wrong microbatch's send. Each direction-plus-microbatch pair gets its own tag.

selfTest.q: Picotron posts single ops with `batch_isend_irecv` and waits immediately. What ordering property does the schedule rely on?
selfTest.a: Every rank calls the same op sequence, so sends and receives pair in program order on the default tag. Any rank-specific branch breaks the pairing and stalls the peer.

selfTest.q: A run hangs after changing `FORWARD_TAG_BASE` on one rank only. What is the first check?
selfTest.a: Tag agreement across peers, then shape and dtype agreement, then a per-rank event log in the TorchFeather schedule-print style to find the unmatched op.

selfTest.q: Where does the pipeline group come from when pipeline composes with data parallelism?
selfTest.a: A subgroup over the pipeline ranks, built with `dist.new_group`. Gradient averaging uses the separate replicate group, never the pipeline group.

study.title: GPipe grid, 1F1B steady state and activation freeing
study.locator: 06:26:15 to 06:38:33: GPipe grid inefficiency, 1F1B warmup into alternating steady state, backward costing about twice a forward for matmul-heavy layers, and why 1F1B frees each microbatch's activations earlier

focus: AFAB keeps both waves sequential: all \(m\) forwards complete before any backward starts, so every stage holds all \(m\) microbatches at the wave boundary.
1F1B starts each microbatch's backward as soon as its loss exists, which alternates one forward with one backward in steady state and frees activations stage by stage.
Warmup on rank \(r\) of \(p\) stages is \(\min(p - 1 - r, m)\): the last stage warms up zero forwards and the first stage warms up the most.
Stored tensors drain first-in first-out: the oldest forward pairs with the incoming gradient, and the cooldown loop exists only to finish the warmup leftovers.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the 1F1B event grid for 3 stages and 4 microbatches: mark warmup, steady state and cooldown on each stage and count each stage's forwards and backwards.
traps: Expecting 1F1B to shrink the bubble at fixed microbatch count. The bubble is the same size as AFAB; the win is bounded activation memory that permits more microbatches.
Starting steady state before microbatch 0 reaches the last stage. No loss exists yet, so early backward calls have no seed gradient.
Forgetting the cooldown. Warmup forwards leave stored tensors behind, and their backward passes still have to run after the last steady-state step.

selfTest.q: A run has 4 stages and 8 microbatches. How many warmup forwards does each rank do?
selfTest.a: \(\min(3 - r, 8)\): ranks 0 to 3 do 3, 2, 1 and 0 warmup forwards.

selfTest.q: Why does the video draw backward blocks about twice as wide as forward blocks?
selfTest.a: A matmul backward needs two matmuls, one for the input gradient and one for the weight gradient, so it costs about twice one forward matmul.

selfTest.q: What work remains after the last 1F1B steady-state iteration on a rank with nonzero warmup?
selfTest.a: One backward per warmup forward, drained oldest-first from the stored tensors: the cooldown phase.

selfTest.q: In the step-8 tutorial diff, what is the structural change from AFAB to 1F1B?
selfTest.a: The single all-backward loop becomes warmup forwards, an alternating forward-backward steady state with paired exchanges, and a cooldown drain of the leftover stored tensors.

study.locator: Sections 2 and 3 (arXiv:2006.09503v3): 1F1B steady state with at most \(p\) microbatches in flight and no weight stashing in the Flush variant, contrasted with GPipe holding all \(m\)

study.title: Bubble figures and transfer on the critical path
study.locator: Pipeline Parallelism section: the 2-stage 2-microbatch bubble figure with data-parallel AllReduces marked, and the transfer-cost figure shifting stages on the critical path

focus: One wave lasts \(T = m + p - 1\) slots: utilization is \(m / (m + p - 1)\) and the idle fraction is \((p - 1) / (m + p - 1)\), for either wave direction.
The book's \((p - 1) / m\) is bubble over ideal compute, an upper bound that exceeds 1 when \(m < p - 1\); use the slot fraction when you need a fraction of total time.
GPipe stashes \(m\) microbatches per stage at the wave boundary; 1F1B keeps at most warmup plus one live per stage, so at most \(p\) on the first stage and 1 on the last.
Backward costing twice forward scales bubble and total together, so the fraction is unchanged under equal stage costs; unequal stages need the critical-stage derivation instead.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive idle fraction \((p - 1) / (m + p - 1)\) and utilization \(m / (m + p - 1)\) for \(p\) stages and \(m\) microbatches, and hand-write the forward schedule for \(p = 2\), \(m = 3\) with cells placed by \(i = t - s\).
traps: Quoting \((p - 1) / m\) as the idle fraction. It is bubble over ideal compute; the idle fraction of total slots is \((p - 1) / (m + p - 1)\).
Assuming 1F1B wastes less compute than AFAB at fixed \(m\). Same bubble; the memory bound is what lets \(m\) grow.
Treating the TensorTonic two-wave model as 1F1B. Its backward wave starts only after the forward wave completes, which is the AFAB shape, not interleaved steady state.

selfTest.q: A run has 4 stages and 8 microbatches. What are the utilization and the idle fraction?
selfTest.a: Utilization \(8 / 11 \approx 0.73\), idle fraction \(3 / 11 \approx 0.27\).

selfTest.q: What is each schedule's peak stashed activation count per stage?
selfTest.a: GPipe holds all \(m\) microbatches at the wave boundary. 1F1B holds at most warmup plus one live per stage, peaking at \(p\) on the first stage.

selfTest.q: Backward costs twice forward on every stage. Does the bubble fraction change?
selfTest.a: No. Both bubble and total scale by the same forward-plus-backward factor, so the fraction stays \((p - 1) / (m + p - 1)\) under equal stage costs.

selfTest.q: Two stages, two microbatches, forward plus backward waves. What are total slots, bubble slots and utilization?
selfTest.a: Total 12, bubble 4, utilization \(8 / 12 \approx 0.67\): each \(T = 3\) wave has 2 useful cells per slot-row pattern giving 8 useful of 12.

study.title: Looped layout and the zero-bubble intro
study.locator: 06:38:54 for the interleaved looped layout with earlier flush and the hop-count cost, and 06:47:59 for the zero-bubble input-gradient versus weight-gradient split intro

focus: Virtual stages cut each device's passes into \(v\) chunks: the bubble shrinks by about \(v\) while each microbatch crosses about \(v\) times more stage boundaries.
Only the input gradient sits on the critical path to earlier stages; the weight gradient waits only for its own input gradient plus the optimizer step, so it fills idle slots.
Depth-first serves earlier microbatches through later stages first; breadth-first serves earlier stages with all ready microbatches first.
Zero bubble is conditional: matched op times, enough microbatches, and bypassed optimizer-step sync all have to hold at once.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, sketch how \(v = 2\) virtual stages per GPU cut the bubble while raising hop count on 4 GPUs, and state the three conditions zero-bubble-class schedules need: the gradient split, matched op times, and optimizer-sync handling.
traps: Calling any interleaved run zero-bubble. Interleaving shrinks the bubble by about \(v\) but keeps one; zero needs the gradient split plus the sync bypass.
Ignoring the extra communication. Each microbatch crosses more stage boundaries, so slow links can eat the schedule win.
Expecting ZBV zero bubble on real layers. It needs forward, input-backward and weight-backward times equal, which real models rarely satisfy.

selfTest.q: Two chunks per GPU: what happens to the bubble and to point-to-point volume?
selfTest.a: The bubble shrinks by about a factor of 2 while P2P volume roughly doubles, since each microbatch crosses twice as many stage boundaries.

selfTest.q: What does the weight gradient wait for, and what does the input gradient unblock?
selfTest.a: The weight gradient waits only for its own input gradient and the optimizer step. The input gradient unblocks the previous stage, so it stays on the critical path while weight gradients fill idle slots.

selfTest.q: How do Interleaved 1F1B and Looped BFS differ when several microbatches are ready?
selfTest.a: Interleaved 1F1B is depth-first: it prioritizes earlier microbatches through later stages. Looped BFS is breadth-first: it prioritizes earlier stages and runs all ready microbatches there.

selfTest.q: What are the ZBV schedule's preconditions?
selfTest.a: Exactly two stages per rank, and the zero-bubble property only when forward, input-backward and weight-backward times match.
